questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how these tests set up the authenticator and its shared state? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
In test_old_failures_age_out_of_the_window, how many failures does the throttle count toward the lockout threshold when the fifth bad password is submitted?
choices: Five, because all failures since the last successful login are counted.
One, because the four earlier failures are older than the 15-minute window and are dropped.
Four, because the fifth failure is only counted after the next request.
Zero, because advancing the clock resets the throttle entirely.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the real-world behaviour of Authenticator.login and LoginThrottle is correct?
choices: Unknown usernames are never counted, so attackers cannot probe for valid accounts through the lockout behaviour.
Locked accounts still have their password hashed, so lockout state cannot be detected by response time.
A lockout applies to the source IP address, so one attacker cannot lock out other users.
Anyone who knows a username can lock that account for 30 minutes by sending five wrong passwords for it.

questions.prompt: After five failures, alice submits the correct password immediately. What happens, and when will a correct password be accepted again?
choices: AccountLocked is raised without checking the password; logins are accepted again once the clock reaches 30 minutes after the fifth failure.
InvalidCredentials is raised because the password hash is compared first; logins are accepted again after the next successful hash comparison.
AccountLocked is raised, and the lock is lifted after 15 minutes when the failure window expires.
The login succeeds, because record_success resets the failure list before the lock is evaluated.
